items.explanation: The 1739 uprising near Charleston terrified planters, who answered with slave codes and harsher discipline meant to deter further revolts.
options: A. A rise in slave imports to the Southern colonies
B. New fortifications around southern cities
C. Efforts to humanize the Middle Passage
D. Harsher treatment of enslaved people across the South
items.stem: A major consequence of the Stono Rebellion was

option_explanations.A: Slave imports did not rise as a result: frightened South Carolina planters did the opposite, imposing a prohibitive duty that cut slave imports for roughly a decade.
option_explanations.B: Building fortifications was not the planters' response. Their answer to the rebellion was tighter control of the enslaved population, not military construction projects.
option_explanations.C: Nothing about the Middle Passage was humanized after Stono. The rebellion produced harsher slave codes, not kinder treatment of captives in transit.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The 1739 Stono Rebellion near Charleston terrified planters, who answered with harsher discipline — South Carolina's 1740 slave code tightened control over every aspect of enslaved people's lives to deter further revolts.

items.explanation: Both England and Spain ran closed mercantilist empires: colonies could trade legally only with the mother country's ships and ports, concentrating profits at home. The Dutch practiced relatively open trade, the Corn Law repeal moved Britain toward free trade, and the Embargo was a temporary diplomatic weapon, not a standing imperial system.
options: A. Spain's restriction of colonial trade to Spanish ships and ports
B. The Dutch Republic's open-port trading policy in the seventeenth century
C. Britain's repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846
D. The American Embargo Act of 1807
items.stem: The Navigation Acts most closely resembled which other imperial trade system?
items.stimulus:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"For the increase of shipping and encouragement of the navigation of this nation, wherein, under the good providence and protection of God, the wealth, safety, and strength of this kingdom is so much concerned... no goods or commodities whatsoever shall be imported into or exported out of any lands... belonging to his Majesty... but in such ships as do truly and without fraud belong only to the people of England..."
—Navigation Act of 1660 (abridged)

option_explanations.A: Correct. Like England, Spain ran a closed mercantilist empire: its colonies could trade legally only with Spanish ships and ports, concentrating the profits at home — the same closed system as the Navigation Acts.
option_explanations.B: The Dutch practiced relatively open, free-trade shipping in the seventeenth century — the opposite of a closed imperial monopoly, and precisely the competition the Navigation Acts targeted.
option_explanations.C: Repealing the Corn Laws in 1846 moved Britain toward free trade — the reverse of the Navigation Acts, which were protectionist restrictions on trade.
option_explanations.D: The Embargo Act of 1807 was a temporary diplomatic weapon Jefferson used against Britain and France, not a standing imperial trade system like the Navigation Acts.
